mainTopic: Proofs that "עין תחת עין" means money, and court cases about appraising injuries
overview: The גמרא keeps testing proofs that "עין תחת עין" means money and not a real eye. It rejects the proofs of רבי דוסתאי בן יהודה and רבי שמעון בן יוחי. Equality is about the sight taken, and a case where the punishment is impossible can simply be exempt. The schools of רבי ישמעאל and רבי חייא learn money from extra phrases in the פסוקים. The proofs of אביי (risk of death), רב זביד (pain) and רב פפא (healing) are each pushed away. רב אשי finally learns it from the word "תחת" in "תחת אשר ענה", which matches as both a person and a damage case. Even רבי אליעזר's "ממש" turns out to mean money, measured by the attacker's own value. Two court stories follow, about a donkey and an ox that injured children. They show that an animal's owner pays only נזק, measured by a slave appraisal. רבא rules that injuries to people are not collected in בבל, and the גמרא begins asking why on the next amud.

steps.title: What about a small person killing a big one?
steps.stepSummary: The rebuttal of רבי דוסתאי continues by pointing to murder, where killer and victim also differ in size.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a small person kills a big person, or a big person kills a small person, how can we execute him? The Torah said 'one law for you,' a law equal for all of you!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is challenging רבי דוסתאי's idea that unequal body parts mean we can't punish with the real thing. It points to murder, where bodies are also unequal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי דוסתאי said that one person's eye may be bigger than another's, so 'eye for eye' can't be literal. But murderers and victims also differ in size, and we still execute. So size differences can't be the reason to switch to money.

keyTerms.meaning: one law, the same for everyone

phrases.english: A small person who killed a large person
and a large person who killed a small person,
how do we execute him?
phrases.notes: Their bodies aren't the same size. So by רבי דוסתאי's reasoning, executing the killer wouldn't be an equal punishment.

phrases.english: The Torah said: "One law shall be for you"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:22

phrases.english: a law that is equal for all of you!

steps.triggerLanguage: קָטָן שֶׁהָרַג אֶת הַגָּדוֹל וְגָדוֹל שֶׁהָרַג אֶת הַקָּטָן, הֵיכִי קָטְלִינַן לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the חכמים's rebuttal of רבי דוסתאי בן יהודה, which began earlier on the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי דוסתאי's claim that unequal body parts force a money payment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Murder also involves unequal bodies, yet the death penalty applies. So inequality of size can't disqualify a literal punishment.

steps.title: Life for life, so sight for sight
steps.stepSummary: Murder is punished because a life was taken, not by size. In the same way, the eye punishment is about taking sight.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he took a life, so the Torah says take a life from him. So too, he took sight, so the Torah says take sight from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why murder works despite size differences, and uses the same logic to reject רבי דוסתאי's proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What counts in murder is the 'life' taken, not body size. Likewise, what counts in 'eye for eye' is the 'sight' taken, which is equal no matter how big the eye is. So רבי דוסתאי's argument falls.

keyTerms.meaning: the Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: Equality is measured by what was taken (life, sight), not by the size of the body part. So רבי דוסתאי's proof is rejected.

phrases.english: Rather, he took a life from him,
so the Merciful One said: take a life from him;
so too, he took sight from him,
so the Merciful One said: take sight from him!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא נְשָׁמָה שְׁקַיל מִינֵּיהּ, נְשָׁמָה אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא נִשְׁקוֹל מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 1 and turns the answer against רבי דוסתאי.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He measured equality by physical size, when it is really measured by the function lost (life or sight).

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says it means money
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says 'eye for eye' means money, and asks whether it could mean a real eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says, 'An eye for an eye' means money. You say money, or maybe it means an actual eye?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that tries to prove 'eye for eye' means money. It sets up the question that רבי שמעון בן יוחי is about to answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a fresh attempt after רבי דוסתאי's proof failed. The question 'or maybe a real eye?' prepares for his proof in the next step.

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא,
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says:
"An eye for an eye" means money.
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:20

phrases.english: You say money,
or does it mean only an actual eye?

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting רבי דוסתאי, the גמרא turns to a different ברייתא with a new proof.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "עין תחת עין" refers to money payment.

steps.title: The blind man who blinds someone
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן יוחי proves his point: a blind or maimed attacker can't lose a real eye or limb, and the law must be equal for all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Suppose a blind man blinded someone, a man missing a limb cut off someone's limb, or a lame man made someone lame. How can I fulfill 'eye for eye' here? And the Torah said 'one law for you,' a law equal for all of you!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון בן יוחי gives his proof. Some attackers have no eye or limb to take, so the punishment must be money for everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the punishment were a real eye, a blind attacker couldn't be punished the same way. Since the Torah demands one equal law, the punishment must be something everyone can pay: money.

keyTerms.meaning: a person missing a hand or limb

phrases.english: Suppose one was blind, and he blinded another;
or was missing a limb, and cut off another's limb;
or was lame, and made another lame;

phrases.aramaic: הֵיאַךְ אֲנִי מְקַיֵּים בָּזֶה ״עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן״ –
phrases.english: how can I fulfill "an eye for an eye" in this case?
And the Torah said: "One law shall be for you,"
a law that is equal for all of you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 3 with a proof.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case of a blind or maimed attacker, combined with "משפט אחד יהיה לכם"

steps.title: Where possible we punish, otherwise we exempt
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים question the proof: maybe we take a real eye when we can, and exempt the attacker when we can't.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: What's the difficulty? Maybe where it's possible, it's possible, and where it's not possible, it's not possible, and we exempt him!
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים push back on רבי שמעון בן יוחי. They suggest the blind attacker is simply exempt, which doesn't prove anything about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having an unusual case where the punishment can't be carried out doesn't force us to change the punishment for everyone. We can punish normal cases literally and exempt the impossible ones.
steps.confusionAlert: Exempting the blind attacker doesn't mean he's paying money instead. It means he gets no bodily punishment at all in that case, so his case doesn't prove the rule is money.

phrases.english: They say: And what is the difficulty?
Perhaps where it is possible, it is possible;
where it is not possible, it is not possible,
and we exempt him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof given in step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבי שמעון בן יוחי's proof
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: An impossible case can be exempted, so 'one law' doesn't force money for everyone.

steps.title: Proof from a טרפה who kills
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים support their point: a טרפה who kills a healthy person shows that sometimes the punishment simply can't apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you don't say this, what do we do with a טרפה who killed a healthy person?
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים back up their claim with the case of a טרפה murderer. Even רבי שמעון בן יוחי must admit that such a case has some exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Murder clearly carries the death penalty, yet a טרפה killer doesn't fit the normal 'equal' pattern. Nobody would say murder is therefore punished with money. So 'one law' must allow exceptions where the punishment isn't possible.

keyTerms.meaning: for if you don't say so
a person with a fatal injury
what do we do to him?

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
a טרפה who killed a healthy person,
phrases.notes: A טרפה here is a person with a fatal injury who is expected to die.

phrases.english: what do we do to him?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי לָא תֵּימָא הָכִי, טְרֵפָה שֶׁהָרַג אֶת הַשָּׁלֵם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rebuttal in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That 'where it's not possible, we exempt' is a valid principle
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case of a טרפה who kills a healthy person

steps.title: Conclusion: we exempt where impossible
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that where the punishment is impossible we exempt, so רבי שמעון בן יוחי's proof is rejected.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, where it's possible, it's possible, and where it's not possible, it's not possible, and we exempt him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up: the principle of the חכמים stands, and רבי שמעון בן יוחי's proof doesn't work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The טרפה case forces us to accept that some cases are simply exempt. Once that's true, a blind attacker's case proves nothing, and his derivation of money falls.
steps.whatToRemember: 'One law for all' doesn't stop us from exempting cases where the punishment can't be carried out. So both רבי דוסתאי's and רבי שמעון בן יוחי's proofs are rejected.

phrases.english: Rather, where it is possible, it is possible;
where it is not possible, it is not possible,
and we exempt him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes from the טרפה proof in step 6 that the principle from step 5 is correct.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Where the punishment can't be carried out, the attacker is exempt. So רבי שמעון בן יוחי's proof that the punishment is money is rejected.

steps.title: The school of רבי ישמעאל: 'giving' means money
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל learns from the words 'so shall it be given to him' that the punishment is money, because 'giving' always means money.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: the פסוק says 'so shall it be given to him.' 'Giving' can only mean money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that 'eye for an eye' means money. The source is a teaching from the school of רבי ישמעאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is built on one word: 'given.' You cannot hand over an eye, but you can hand over money. So the Torah must mean that the attacker pays.

keyTerms.meaning: The school of (a teacher's study hall)

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
The verse says: "so shall it be given to him"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:20

phrases.english: and 'giving' can only mean money.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל תָּנָא, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבי שמעון בן יוחי's proof was rejected, the גמרא brings a new source for the same idea.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'So shall it be given to him' teaches that the attacker pays money, since giving means money.

steps.title: But the same verse uses 'give' for a real injury
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the same פסוק says 'as he gives a blemish to a person,' and that clearly means a real injury, not money.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, when it says 'as he gives a blemish to a person,' is that also money?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the proof from step 8. The same פסוק uses the word 'give' for the actual wound, which has nothing to do with money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'giving' always means money, then 'as he gives a blemish' would also have to mean money. That makes no sense, because the attacker actually injured someone. So the word 'give' alone cannot prove anything.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (a challenge that pushes your logic further)

phrases.english: But if so,
"as he gives a blemish to a person"
phrases.notes: These are the earlier words of the same פסוק, ויקרא 24:20. Here 'gives' plainly means he caused a real wound.

phrases.english: is that also money?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the word 'giving' always means money.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same פסוק uses 'give' for a physical injury, so the word cannot automatically mean money.

steps.title: The proof comes from an extra verse
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the school of רבי ישמעאל learns from the fact that 'so shall it be given to him' is extra, because the previous פסוק already said 'as he did, so shall be done to him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: the school of רבי ישמעאל learns from an extra verse. The Torah already wrote: 'If a man gives a blemish to his fellow, as he did, so shall be done to him.' So why do I need 'so shall it be given to him'? Learn from it: money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the school of רבי ישמעאל. Their proof is not from the word 'give' by itself, but from a phrase that would otherwise be unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פסוק 19 already told us the punishment: 'as he did, so shall be done to him.' Repeating it in פסוק 20 with 'so shall it be given to him' seems extra. That extra phrase is what teaches the new idea of money.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the shift here. The proof is no longer 'giving means money' all by itself. It is now 'this phrase is extra, so it must teach something, and with the word giving, it teaches money.'

phrases.english: They say: The school of Rabbi Yishmael
learns from an extra verse.
After all, it is written:
"And if a man gives a blemish to his fellow,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:19

phrases.english: as he did, so shall be done to him."
So why do I need "so shall it be given to him"?
Learn from it: money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל קְרָא יַתִּירָא דָּרְשִׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9 by explaining where the proof really comes from.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the source of the proof (an extra phrase, not the meaning of one word)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The proof seemed to rest only on the meaning of the word 'give.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The proof rests on the extra phrase 'so shall it be given to him,' since פסוק 19 already gave the punishment.

steps.title: Then why write 'as he gives a blemish'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if 'given' teaches money, why did the Torah use giving language for the injury itself?
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need 'as he gives a blemish to a person'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the leftover phrase from step 9. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Using the word 'give' for the injury seems strange if giving is meant to point to money. The גמרא wants to know what that wording is doing there.

phrases.english: Why do I need "as he gives a blemish to a person"?

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּאֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מוּם בָּאָדָם לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the answer of step 10 by asking about the phrase used in the challenge of step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the Torah used the word 'give' for the physical injury.

steps.title: It was written to match the style
steps.stepSummary: Because the Torah needed to write 'so shall it be given to him,' it also used 'as he gives' earlier in the פסוק, so the wording matches.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the Torah needed to write 'so shall it be given to him,' it also wrote 'as he gives a blemish to a person.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'gives' in the first half of the פסוק does not teach anything. It is there to match the second half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only 'so shall it be given to him' carries the lesson of money. 'As he gives a blemish' just copies the same style of wording. So it does not hurt the proof.
steps.whatToRemember: The school of רבי ישמעאל: 'so shall it be given to him' is an extra phrase, so it teaches money. 'As he gives a blemish' is only written to match the style.

phrases.english: Since it needed to write "so shall it be given to him,"
it also wrote "as he gives a blemish to a person."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'gives' about the injury is only there to match the giving language that comes after it.

steps.title: The school of רבי חייא: 'hand for hand' means money
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי חייא learns from 'hand for hand' that the punishment is something passed from hand to hand, which is money.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי חייא taught: the פסוק says 'hand for hand.' That means something given from hand to hand. What is that? Money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another source that 'eye for an eye' means money. This source is a teaching from the school of רבי חייא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'יד ביד' are read as 'from hand into hand,' meaning a payment handed over. The thing usually handed from one person to another is money.

keyTerms.meaning: Hand for hand (read here as 'hand into hand')

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Chiya taught:
The verse says: "hand for hand"
phrases.notes: דברים 19:21. This פסוק is about witnesses caught lying (עדים זוממין).

phrases.english: something that is given from hand to hand.
And what is that? Money.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא תָּנָא, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate source for the same idea as step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Hand for hand' means something passed from hand to hand, which is money.

steps.title: Then what about 'foot for foot'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the same פסוק says 'foot for foot.' Does that also mean something passed from foot to foot?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, is 'foot for foot' also like that?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the proof from step 13. The same reading does not work on the very next phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is passed 'from foot to foot.' So reading 'יד ביד' as handing over money seems forced, since 'foot for foot' cannot be read that way.

phrases.english: But if so,
is "foot for foot" also like that?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, רֶגֶל בְּרָגֶל נָמֵי הָכִי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of step 13, just as step 9 challenged step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading 'hand for hand' as 'given from hand to hand.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The matching phrase 'foot for foot' cannot mean something passed from foot to foot.

steps.title: Again, the proof comes from an extra phrase
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי חייא learns from an extra phrase. The Torah already said 'do to him as he plotted to do to his brother,' so 'hand for hand' is not needed for a real punishment and must teach money.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: the school of רבי חייא learns from an extra verse. The Torah already wrote: 'You shall do to him as he plotted to do to his brother.' If you think it means literally, why do I need 'hand for hand'? Learn from it: money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the school of רבי חייא the same way it defended the school of רבי ישמעאל. The proof comes from an unnecessary phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the Torah already said the lying witnesses get whatever they plotted to do. If the punishment were a real hand, 'hand for hand' would add nothing. Since it is extra, it teaches that the punishment is money.

phrases.english: They say: The school of Rabbi Chiya
is learning from an extra verse.
After all, it is written:
"You shall do to him as he plotted to do to his brother."
phrases.notes: דברים 19:19

phrases.english: If you think it means literally,
why do I need "hand for hand"?
Learn from it: money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: דְּבֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא קְרָא יַתִּירָא קָא דָרְשִׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the source of the proof (an extra phrase)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The proof seemed to rest only on reading 'hand for hand' as handing something over.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since 'do to him as he plotted' already covers the punishment, 'hand for hand' is extra and teaches money.

steps.title: Then why write 'foot for foot'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if 'hand for hand' teaches money, what is 'foot for foot' doing in the פסוק?
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need 'foot for foot'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the leftover phrase from step 14. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Foot for foot' also looks extra, but it cannot be read as 'passed from foot to foot.' So the גמרא asks why it was written.

phrases.english: Why do I need "foot for foot"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the answer of step 15, just as step 11 followed step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the Torah wrote 'foot for foot' if only 'hand for hand' teaches money.

steps.title: 'Foot for foot' was written to match
steps.stepSummary: Because the Torah wrote 'hand for hand,' it also wrote 'foot for foot' to keep the same pattern.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since it wrote 'hand for hand,' it also wrote 'foot for foot.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'foot for foot' does not teach anything new. It just follows the pattern of 'hand for hand.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only 'hand for hand' carries the lesson of money. 'Foot for foot' is written alongside it for style. So the challenge from step 14 falls away.
steps.whatToRemember: Both schools use the same method. The Torah has an extra phrase ('so shall it be given to him' or 'hand for hand') that teaches money. The matching phrase next to it ('as he gives a blemish' or 'foot for foot') is only there for style.

phrases.english: Since it wrote "hand for hand,"
it also wrote "foot for foot."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Foot for foot' is written only to match 'hand for hand.'

steps.title: אביי's proof: never an eye and a life for one eye
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a proof from the school of חזקיה. The Torah says 'an eye for an eye' and 'a life for a life,' but never a life and an eye for an eye. If the punishment were a real blinding, the attacker might die from it, so he would lose both.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי says: It comes from what the school of חזקיה taught. The school of חזקיה taught: 'An eye for an eye'; 'A life for a life,' but not a life and an eye for an eye. If you think it means a real eye, sometimes you would get an eye and a life for an eye, because while they blind him, his soul leaves him.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a new source that ״עין תחת עין״ means money. His reason is that a real blinding could end up costing the attacker his life as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's measure is exact: one eye for one eye. A real blinding risks taking more than the Torah allows, because the attacker might die from it. So the punishment must be money, which can never 'overshoot.'

keyTerms.meaning: It comes from, it is learned from

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּיֵי אוֹמֵר: אָתְיָא מִדְּתָנֵי דְּבֵי חִזְקִיָּה,
phrases.english: Abaye says: It comes from what the school of Ḥizkiyya taught,
as the school of Ḥizkiyya taught:
"An eye for an eye";
phrases.notes: שמות 21:24

phrases.english: "A life for a life" –
phrases.notes: שמות 21:23

phrases.english: but not a life and an eye for an eye.
And if you think it means literally,
there are times when you would find
an eye and a life for an eye –
since while they blind him,
his soul leaves him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אביי אומר: אתיא מדתני דבי חזקיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the school of רבי חייא's proof, the גמרא brings a new, separate proof from אביי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A literal blinding could take a life along with an eye, which the Torah does not allow; so ״עין תחת עין״ means money.

steps.title: The court could check first if he can survive
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects אביי's proof. The court could first estimate whether the attacker can survive a blinding. If he can, they do it; if not, they don't. And if they judged he could survive but he dies anyway, then he dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difficulty? Maybe we evaluate him. If he can withstand it, we do it, and if he cannot withstand it, we don't do it. And if we evaluate that he can withstand it, and we do it and his soul leaves him, if he dies, let him die!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on אביי. The risk of death is not a real problem, because the court can check the attacker's strength before blinding him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי assumed a literal blinding would sometimes kill. The גמרא answers that the court can avoid this by assessing him first. And if he dies after a careful assessment, that is not considered the court taking 'a life for an eye.'

keyTerms.meaning: And what is the difficulty? (this is no real problem)
We do it (carry out the punishment)

phrases.english: And what is the difficulty?
Perhaps we evaluate him;
if he can withstand it – we do it,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא מָצֵי מְקַבֵּל – לָא עָבְדִינַן;
phrases.english: and if he cannot withstand it – we do not do it;
and if we evaluate that he can withstand it,
and we do it to him and his spirit departs –
if he dies, let him die!

steps.triggerLanguage: ומאי קושיא? דלמא מימד אמדינן ליה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reasoning behind אביי's proof in step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects אביי's proof completely, though not the conclusion that ״עין תחת עין״ means money.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: אביי assumed death would be the Torah's fault, but the court can assess the attacker first, and a death after a proper assessment is not counted against the court.

steps.title: Support from the law of מלקות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its rejection with a משנה about מלקות. If the court estimated how many lashes a person could take and he died anyway, the one giving the lashes is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't we learn about lashes: If they evaluated him and he died under his hand, he is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its point with a משנה about lashes. It shows that this 'assess first, and if he dies, he dies' approach already exists in halacha.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With מלקות too, the punishment is not meant to kill. Still, if the court assessed him properly and he died, nobody is blamed. The same could work for a literal blinding, so אביי's proof falls away.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי's proof is rejected: the court can assess the attacker first, just like with מלקות.

phrases.english: Didn't we learn with regard to lashes:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in מכות 22b.

phrases.english: If they evaluated him, and he died under his hand – he is exempt?
phrases.notes: 'His hand' means the hand of the court officer giving the lashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to support the rejection made in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that a death after a proper court assessment does not count as an extra punishment.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about מלקות: if they assessed him and he died, the officer is exempt.

steps.title: רב זביד's proof from 'a wound for a wound'
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבה says that ״פצע תחת פצע״ teaches that the attacker pays for pain even when he also pays for damage. If the punishment were a real blinding, the attacker would feel pain just like the victim, so why pay extra for pain?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבה: The verse says, 'A wound for a wound,' to give payment for pain along with payment for damage. And if you think it means a real eye, just as this one has pain, that one also has pain!
steps.whatsHappening: A new proof is offered. The Torah requires a separate payment for pain, which only makes sense if the main punishment is money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the attacker's eye were really taken, he would suffer the same pain as the victim, and things would be even. So there would be no reason for an extra pain payment. Since the Torah requires one, ״עין תחת עין״ must mean money for the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Pain (one of the payments for injury)

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rabba,
the verse states: "A wound for a wound" –
phrases.notes: שמות 21:25

phrases.english: to give payment for pain where there is payment for damage.
And if you think it means literally –

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דִּלְהַאי הָוֵי לֵיהּ צַעֲרָא,
phrases.english: just as this one has pain,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the victim, and 'that one' in the next line is the attacker.

phrases.english: that one also has pain!

steps.triggerLanguage: רב זביד משמיה דרבה אמר, אמר קרא: פצע תחת פצע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After אביי's proof was rejected, a new proof is brought.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since the Torah requires a separate pain payment, the main punishment for an eye must be money and not a real blinding.

steps.title: People feel pain differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רב זביד's proof. Some people are delicate and feel more pain, and some are not delicate and feel less. So even with a real blinding, the pain would not always be equal.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difficulty? Maybe there is a person who is delicate and has more pain, and there is a person who is not delicate and does not have pain!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב זביד. Two people losing an eye don't necessarily feel the same amount of pain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב זביד assumed the attacker's pain would exactly match the victim's. The גמרא points out that pain depends on the person. So even with a literal blinding, a pain payment could still be needed.

phrases.english: And what is the difficulty?
Perhaps there is a person who is delicate –
he has more pain,
and there is a person who is not delicate –
he does not have pain!
phrases.notes: He means he doesn't feel as much pain.

steps.triggerLanguage: ומאי קושיא? דלמא איכא איניש דמפנק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reasoning behind רב זביד's proof in step 21.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב זביד's proof, not the conclusion that ״עין תחת עין״ means money.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב זביד assumed the attacker and the victim would feel equal pain, but pain differs from person to person.

steps.title: So what would the pain payment be for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference the pain payment would make if the attacker's eye were really taken.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the practical difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next line. If the eye is really taken, what exactly would the pain payment cover?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having said that pain levels differ, the גמרא wants to spell out what the payment would actually do in that case. The answer comes in the next step.

phrases.english: What is the practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the rejection in step 22 by asking what the pain payment would accomplish.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the pain payment would cover if the attacker's eye were really taken.

steps.title: He pays the difference in pain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the attacker would pay the difference between the victim's pain and his own. So ״פצע תחת פצע״ still makes sense even with a literal blinding, and רב זביד's proof falls away.
steps.simpleTranslation: To give him the difference between them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The pain payment would cover the gap between how much the victim suffered and how much the attacker suffered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the pain is not equal, the extra payment evens it out. So ״פצע תחת פצע״ does not prove that ״עין תחת עין״ means money. רב זביד's proof is rejected, just like אביי's.

keyTerms.meaning: In between; the difference between them

steps.whatToRemember: Both אביי's proof (risk of death) and רב זביד's proof (payment for pain) are rejected. The court can assess the attacker first, and pain can differ, so neither proof forces ״עין תחת עין״ to mean money.

phrases.english: To give him that which is in between.
phrases.notes: He pays only for the extra pain the victim felt beyond what the attacker felt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 23 and finishes the rejection of רב זביד's proof.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The pain payment would cover the difference between the victim's pain and the attacker's pain.

steps.title: רב פפא's proof from the healing payment
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא, quoting רבא, says "ורפא ירפא" teaches that the attacker pays medical costs even when he also pays for damage. If the eye were literally taken, the attacker would need a doctor too, so why pay extra for healing?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said in the name of רבא: The פסוק says "and he shall surely heal him." This teaches that the attacker pays for healing even where he also pays for damage. If you think the punishment is a real blinding, then just as the victim needs a doctor, the attacker also needs a doctor!
steps.whatsHappening: A new proof that "עין תחת עין" means money. It works the same way as רב זביד's proof from pain, but this time it uses the medical bills.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah makes the attacker pay רפוי (medical costs) on top of נזק (damage). If the attacker's eye were really taken, both people would have doctor bills, and it would make no sense for one to pay the other's. So the extra healing payment shows the Torah means money.

keyTerms.meaning: "And he shall surely heal": the פסוק that makes the attacker pay medical costs
Healing; the payment for medical costs
Damage; the payment for the lost value of the body part

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said in the name of Rava:
The verse says: "And he shall surely heal him"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:19

phrases.english: to pay for healing even where he pays for damage.
And if it enters your mind that it means literally,
then just as this one needs a doctor,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the victim who was injured.

phrases.english: this one also needs a doctor!
phrases.notes: Now "this one" is the attacker, whose eye the court would have taken.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא אָמַר, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב זביד's proof from pain is pushed away, a new proof built the same way is brought from the healing payment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The extra healing payment shows that "עין תחת עין" means money, since a literal blinding would leave both sides needing medical care.

steps.title: People heal at different speeds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רב פפא's proof. Some people's flesh heals quickly and some heal slowly, so the medical costs would not be equal even with a real blinding.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difficulty? Maybe there is someone whose flesh heals quickly, and there is someone whose flesh does not heal quickly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away רב פפא's proof, the same way it pushed away רב זביד's proof about pain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed both sides would have equal medical needs. But healing speed is different for each person, so the victim may need much more care than the attacker. A healing payment could still make sense with a literal blinding.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difficulty? (the proof is not convincing)

phrases.english: What is the difficulty?
Perhaps there is one whose flesh heals quickly,
and there is one whose flesh does not heal quickly!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 25 with the same kind of argument used in step 22.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof of רב פפא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It wrongly assumes the victim and the attacker would heal equally.

steps.title: What would the healing payment change?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference the healing payment would make if the eye were really taken.
steps.simpleTranslation: What practical difference does it make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question, setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we say both sides may heal differently, we need to know what exactly the attacker pays under a literal reading. This question is the same one asked about pain in step 23.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference comes out of it?

phrases.english: What is the practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the rejection in step 26 would work in practice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the healing payment would be for if the attacker's eye were literally taken.

steps.title: He pays the difference in medical costs
steps.stepSummary: The attacker would pay the difference between the victim's medical costs and his own. So "ורפא ירפא" still makes sense with a literal blinding, and רב פפא's proof falls away.
steps.simpleTranslation: To give him the difference between them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: the healing payment would cover only the gap between the two people's medical needs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a literal blinding, the attacker would pay only the extra medical cost the victim has beyond his own. Because the פסוק can be explained this way, it does not prove that the Torah means money.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רב זביד's proof (pain) and רב פפא's proof (healing) are pushed away the same way: people differ, so the attacker would pay the difference.

phrases.english: To give him
that which is the difference in between.
phrases.notes: He means the extra medical cost the victim has beyond what the attacker needs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27 and closes the rejection of רב פפא's proof.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The attacker pays the difference between the victim's medical costs and his own.

steps.title: רב אשי: "תחת" from the ox teaches money
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי learns from a גזירה שוה that "עין תחת עין" means money. The word "תחת" appears by the ox ("שור תחת השור"), where it clearly means money, so it means money here too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: We learn "for" (תחת) from "for" by an ox. It is written here: "an eye for an eye," and it is written there: "he shall surely pay an ox for the ox." Just as there it means money, so too here it means money.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי brings a new proof that "עין תחת עין" means money, using a word link between two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By an ox that killed another ox, "שור תחת השור" means the owner pays the value, not a real ox. Since the same word "תחת" appears by injuries, רב אשי says it carries the same meaning: money.

keyTerms.meaning: Learning one law from another because the same word appears in both
"He shall surely pay an ox for the ox"

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is learned from "for" and "for" from an ox;
phrases.notes: The same word "תחת" appears in both פסוקים, so one teaches about the other.

phrases.english: It is written here: "An eye for an eye,"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:24

phrases.english: and it is written there:
"He shall surely pay an ox for the ox"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:36

phrases.english: just as there it means money,
so too here it means money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proofs from pain and healing are pushed away, רב אשי brings a completely different kind of proof, a word link.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "תחת" by injuries means money, just like "תחת" by the ox.

steps.title: Why not learn "תחת" from the murderer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב אשי: why link "תחת" to the ox? Link it instead to "נפש תחת נפש" by a person who kills, where it means literally taking a life.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did you see that made you learn "for" from "for" by an ox? Let us learn "for" from "for" by a person, as it is written: "You shall give a life for a life." Just as there it is literal, so too here it is literal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב אשי's word link by showing that the same word "תחת" also appears where it means literally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A word link only works if we know which source to link to. "נפש תחת נפש" is also about a person hurting a person, and there the punishment is real. So the word "תחת" alone could point to a literal blinding just as easily as to money.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see? (why choose this option over the other?)

phrases.english: What did you see that you learn
"for" and "for" from an ox?
Let us learn "for" and "for" from a person,
as it is written: "And you shall give a life for a life";
phrases.notes: שמות 21:23

phrases.english: just as there it is literal,
so too here it is literal!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's word link from step 29 by offering a different source for the same word.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's choice to link "תחת" to the ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same word "תחת" appears by a person who kills, where it means literally, so the link could just as well prove a literal blinding.

steps.title: Learn damages from damages, not from death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge to רב אשי: an injury case should be learned from another damage case (the ox), not from a case of killing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: we learn damages from damages, and we do not learn damages from death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב אשי's link to the ox. An eye injury is a damage case, so it should be compared to another damage case, not to a killing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 30 someone said: link "תחת" to "נפש תחת נפש", where it means literally taking a life. The answer is that the ox case and the eye case are both about damage, while "נפש תחת נפש" is about death. So the ox is the better match.

phrases.english: They say: we learn damages from damages,
and we do not learn damages from death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Picks the better match for the גזירה שוה by subject matter (damage vs. death)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "תחת" could be learned from "נפש תחת נפש", which would mean a literal punishment.
steps.terutzMaskana: Damage should be learned from damage, so the ox case (money) is the right source.

steps.title: On the contrary: learn a person from a person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the logic around: the eye case is about a person, so learn it from "נפש תחת נפש" (a person), not from an animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! We should learn a person from a person, and not learn a person from an animal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. There is another way to pick the closest match, and it points the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Yes, the ox case is about damage, but it is about an animal. "נפש תחת נפש" is about a human being, just like the eye case. By this measure the closer source means a literal punishment, so רב אשי's proof is stuck.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary, the opposite is true

phrases.english: On the contrary! We learn a person from a person,
and we do not learn a person from an animal!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 31 by using a different way of judging similarity.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 31 that the ox is the best source for the גזירה שוה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Matching by person vs. animal is just as strong as matching by damage vs. death, and it favors "נפש תחת נפש".

steps.title: רב אשי's new source: "תחת אשר ענה"
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי switches sources. He learns "תחת" from the man who violated a girl ("תחת אשר ענה"), which is about a person and about damage, and there the payment is money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: he learns it from "because (תחת) he afflicted her." That is learning a person from a person, and damages from damages.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי drops the ox and gives a new source for the word "תחת", one that fits on both counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case of "תחת אשר ענה" the man pays fifty shekels, so "תחת" there means money. That case is about a human victim and about harm done to her. So it matches the eye case both ways, and "עין תחת עין" means money.

keyTerms.meaning: "Because he afflicted her", said of a man who violates a girl
Learning one law from another because the same word appears in both

steps.whatToRemember: The final source for "עין תחת עין" = money in this line is "תחת אשר ענה", because it matches both as a person and as damage.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a גזירה שוה works best when the two cases are alike in every important way, and that the גמרא will drop a weaker match for a stronger one.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
He learns it from "because he afflicted her",
phrases.notes: דברים 22:29. There the man pays fifty shekels of silver, so "תחת" means money.

phrases.english: a person from a person, and damages from damages.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: מִ״תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר עִנָּהּ״ יָלֵיף לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the ox-based גזירה שוה that was weakened in step 32.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "עין תחת עין" means money, learned from "תחת אשר ענה", which matches as both a person and a damage case.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: "an eye for an eye" means actually
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי אליעזר saying that "עין תחת עין" means "ממש", actually.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי אליעזר says: "An eye for an eye" means actually.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source, a ברייתא, that seems to say the verse should be read literally. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now every view has said the verse means money. רבי אליעזר's word "ממש" sounds like he wants the attacker's real eye taken. The גמרא will now figure out what he meant.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer says:
"An eye for an eye" means actually.
phrases.notes: שמות 21:24.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: ״עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן״ – מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new section with a ברייתא that seems to go against all the earlier proofs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר says "עין תחת עין" is "ממש".

steps.title: Could רבי אליעזר really mean a literal eye?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is shocked: does רבי אליעזר really disagree with all the other תנאים who said the verse means money?
steps.simpleTranslation: "Actually"? Can you really think that? Does רבי אליעזר not agree with all these תנאים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא refuses to accept that רבי אליעזר wants a real eye taken, because every other תנא says it means money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Many תנאים brought proofs that the verse means money. It is hard to believe רבי אליעזר stands alone against all of them. So "ממש" must mean something else, and the גמרא now has to explain it.

keyTerms.meaning: תנאים, the Sages of the משנה era

phrases.english: "Actually"? Would you really think so?!

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר לֵית לֵיהּ כְּכֹל הָנֵי תַּנָּאֵי?!
phrases.english: Does Rabbi Eliezer not hold like all these tanna'im?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the plain reading of רבי אליעזר's statement in step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading רבי אליעזר's "ממש" as a literal eye
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That would set him alone against all the other תנאים, which is not likely.

steps.title: רבה: don't value him as a slave
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that "ממש" only means the victim is not valued as a slave when working out the payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: it comes to say that we do not value him as a slave.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a first answer. רבי אליעזר agrees it is money, and "ממש" is about how the amount is worked out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the court figures the payment by asking how much the victim would drop in value as a slave. רבה says "ממש" means the court does not use that slave-value method. So רבי אליעזר still holds the payment is money.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
It comes to say that we do not value him as a slave.
phrases.notes: "Him" is the injured person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין שָׁמִין אוֹתוֹ כְּעֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reads "ממש" as a rule about how to measure the payment
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אליעזר wants the attacker's real eye taken.
steps.terutzMaskana: He agrees it is money; he only means the victim is not valued as a slave.

steps.title: אביי: then how do you value him?
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבה: if not as a slave, then as a free man? A free man has no price.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Then like whom? Like a free man? Does a free man have a price?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's answer. If you take away the slave method, there is nothing left to measure the damage with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A free person cannot be bought or sold, so he has no market value. The only way to put a number on an injury is to imagine him as a slave. So רבה's reading leaves the court with no way to set the payment.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
Then like whom? Like a free man?!

phrases.aramaic: בֶּן חוֹרִין מִי אִית לֵיהּ דָּמֵי?
phrases.english: Does a free man have a price?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אֶלָּא כְּמַאן, כְּבֶן חוֹרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's answer in step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's reading that the victim is not valued as a slave
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without slave-value there is no way to price a free man's injury.

steps.title: רב אשי: value the attacker, not the victim
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains "ממש": the court does not value the victim's loss. It values how much the attacker would lose with the same injury.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: it comes to say that we do not value him by the injured person, but by the one who did the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a better answer that solves אביי's problem. "ממש" means the measuring is done on the attacker himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court still uses a slave-value method, so אביי's question is answered. But it measures the attacker: how much less would he be worth with the same injury? That is "ממש", his own eye for the eye he took. The payment is still money.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who did the damage

steps.whatToRemember: Even רבי אליעזר agrees "עין תחת עין" means money. In רב אשי's reading, "ממש" only means the payment is measured by the attacker's own eye.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read "ממש" as taking out a real eye. In רב אשי's reading it is about whose value is measured, and the payment is still money.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
It comes to say that we do not value it by the injured person,
but rather by the one who did the damage.
phrases.notes: The court asks how much the attacker's own value would drop with the same injury, and he pays that.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין שָׁמִין אוֹתוֹ בְּנִיזָּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבה's answer, which אביי rejected in step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reads "ממש" as measuring the attacker's value instead of the victim's
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "ממש" means not valuing as a slave at all (רבה), which leaves no way to set a price.
steps.terutzMaskana: "ממש" means the payment is measured by what the attacker would lose; it is still money.

steps.title: A donkey cuts off a child's hand
steps.stepSummary: A donkey cut off a child's hand. רב פפא בר שמואל tells the court officers to assess four types of payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a donkey that cut off a child's hand. The case came before רב פפא בר שמואל. He told the officers: go assess four kinds of payment for the child.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a real-life court story. רב פפא בר שמואל gives his first ruling, and the next steps will challenge it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists five payments for injuring a person: נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת. רב פפא בר שמואל orders only four, which sets up the coming questions.

keyTerms.meaning: Four things, meaning four types of payment

phrases.english: There was a certain donkey that cut off a child's hand.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל,
phrases.english: The case came before Rav Pappa bar Shmuel.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: זִילוּ שׁוּמוּ לֵיהּ אַרְבָּעָה דְּבָרִים.
phrases.english: He said to them: Go assess four things for him.
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the court officers who do the appraising.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the meaning of 'עין תחת עין' to a practical court case about injury payments.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא בר שמואל initially rules that four types of payment should be assessed for the injured child.

steps.title: רבא objects: the משנה lists five
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges the ruling: the משנה teaches five payments, not four.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: But we learned in the משנה that there are five payments!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא points out that the number four does not match the משנה, which lists five payments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is simple: a known source says five, and the ruling says four. So רב פפא בר שמואל has to explain which payment he left out and why.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
But we learned five!
phrases.notes: He means the משנה that lists five payments for injuring a person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of four payments in step 39.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא בר שמואל's instruction to assess four payments.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה explicitly lists five payments, so ordering four seems to leave one out.

steps.title: Four besides the damage itself
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא בר שמואל explains he meant four payments in addition to נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I was speaking about the four besides נזק.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא בר שמואל clarifies his words: he did not drop a payment. He meant four on top of נזק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the total is still five, exactly like the משנה. 'Four' referred only to צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת, with נזק understood as obvious.

phrases.english: He said to him: I was saying four besides the damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's objection in step 40.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifying his wording: four in addition to נזק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He seemed to be leaving out one of the five payments.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant all five: נזק plus four others.

steps.title: אביי objects: a donkey pays only damage
steps.stepSummary: אביי points out that when an animal injures, the owner pays only נזק, not the other four payments.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: But this was a donkey, and a donkey pays only נזק!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks the ruling from a new direction. The injury came from an animal, not a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The five payments apply when a person injures someone. When an animal causes the injury, its owner pays only נזק. So the extra four payments should not be charged at all.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
But it is a donkey,
and a donkey pays only for damage!
phrases.notes: He means the donkey's owner, who pays for what his animal did.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא חֲמוֹר הוּא וַחֲמוֹר אֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם אֶלָּא נֶזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 41 confirmed all five payments, אביי challenges charging the extra four at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: Charging four payments beyond נזק for an injury caused by a donkey.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An animal's owner is liable only for נזק, so צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת do not apply.

steps.title: Assess only the damage
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא בר שמואל accepts אביי's point and orders only נזק to be assessed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Go assess his נזק.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא בר שמואל accepts the challenge and changes his instruction: only the damage gets assessed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a defense of the earlier ruling but a correction of it. The four extra payments are dropped, and only נזק remains.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: זִילוּ שׁוּמוּ לֵיהּ נִזְקֵיהּ.
phrases.english: He said to them: Go assess his damage for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to אביי in step 42 by accepting the objection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Concession: the ruling is changed to match the objection.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only נזק is assessed for an injury caused by a donkey.

steps.title: The damage must be measured as a slave
steps.stepSummary: An objection: נזק has to be measured by valuing the child as if he were a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he needs to be appraised as a slave!
steps.whatsHappening: Someone points out that 'assess his damage' is not specific enough. נזק is measured in a particular way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נזק is calculated by asking how much less this person would be worth as a slave after the injury. The objection insists the instruction say this clearly.

phrases.english: But he needs to be appraised as a slave!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refines the instruction of step 43 about how to assess נזק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The general instruction 'go assess his damage'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: נזק is measured by valuing the victim as a slave, so the instruction must reflect this method.

steps.title: Appraise him as a slave
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא בר שמואל agrees and orders the child to be appraised as a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Go appraise him as a slave.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא בר שמואל accepts the point and gives his final instruction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After אביי's objection and the point about the slave appraisal, the ruling is now complete: only נזק, measured by the slave appraisal. This sets up the father's reaction in the next step.
steps.whatToRemember: For an injury caused by an animal, the owner pays only נזק, and נזק is measured by appraising the victim as a slave.

phrases.english: He said to them: Go appraise him as a slave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the objection of step 44.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Concession: adopts the slave appraisal method.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Assess the damage in a general way.
steps.terutzMaskana: Assess the child's נזק by valuing him as a slave.

steps.title: The father refuses the slave appraisal
steps.stepSummary: The child's father does not want his son appraised as a slave because it is demeaning.
steps.simpleTranslation: The child's father said to them: I don't want this, because it is degrading for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The father objects to the slave appraisal, and the court will respond next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father's concern is the child's dignity, not the law. He would rather give up the payment than have his son valued like a slave.

keyTerms.meaning: Because the matter is degrading for him

phrases.english: The child's father said to them:
I do not want it, because the matter is degrading for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the final ruling of step 45.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The father refuses to have his child appraised as a slave.

steps.title: You are hurting the child
steps.stepSummary: The court tells the father that refusing will cost the child his compensation.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: But you are causing a loss to the child!
steps.whatsHappening: The court pushes back on the father. Without the appraisal, the child gets no payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The money really belongs to the injured child. So the father's refusal looks like he is giving away something that is not his.

keyTerms.meaning: You are causing a loss, harming

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: וְהָא קָא מְחַיְּיבַתְּ לֵיהּ לְיָנוֹקָא!
phrases.english: They said to him: But you are causing a loss to the child!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the father's refusal in step 46.
steps.kashyaTarget: The father's refusal of the appraisal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The compensation belongs to the child, so refusing it harms him.

steps.title: I will repay him myself
steps.stepSummary: The father answers that when the child grows up, he will make it up to him from his own money.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: When he grows up, I will make it up to him from my own money.
steps.whatsHappening: The father answers the court's objection and ends the first story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The child loses nothing in the end, because the father will cover the loss himself. This protects both the child's dignity and his money.

keyTerms.meaning: I will appease him, make it up to him

phrases.english: He said to them: When he grows up,
I will appease him from my own money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the court's objection in step 47.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The loss is removed because the father will pay it himself.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Refusing the appraisal causes the child to lose money.
steps.terutzMaskana: The child will be compensated later from the father's own money.

steps.title: An ox chews a child's hand
steps.stepSummary: An ox chewed a child's hand. רבא orders the child to be appraised as a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an ox that chewed a child's hand. The case came before רבא. He told them: go appraise him as a slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second, similar story. רבא's ruling here will be questioned next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the donkey case, an animal caused the injury, so only נזק applies, measured by the slave appraisal. The question will be whether this ruling fits רבא's own view.

phrases.english: There was a certain ox that chewed a child's hand.
The case came before Rava.
He said to them: Go appraise him as a slave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second court story with a similar injury.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא orders the injured child to be appraised as a slave.

steps.title: Didn't רבא say this is not collected in בבל?
steps.stepSummary: They challenge רבא with his own rule that payments based on slave appraisal are not collected in בבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: But you, Master, said that anything appraised as a slave is not collected in בבל!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא is challenged with his own words. If בבל courts don't collect this payment, why bother appraising?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא himself taught that injuries measured by a slave appraisal are not collected by courts in בבל. So his order to appraise seems pointless.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: וְהָא מָר הוּא דְּאָמַר:
phrases.english: They said to him: But wasn't it the Master who said:
Anyone who is appraised as a slave,
we do not collect it in Babylonia!
phrases.notes: 'It' means the payment worked out through that appraisal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's ruling in step 49.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's order to appraise the child as a slave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא himself holds that such payments are not collected in בבל, so the appraisal seems useless.

steps.title: It matters if the victim seizes
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the appraisal is needed for a case where the victim seizes property from the ox's owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: It is needed for a case where he seized property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains why the appraisal still has a purpose even though the court won't collect it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court won't force payment, but if the victim grabs property on his own, the court won't make him give it back. The appraisal tells us how much he is allowed to keep.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for, or it is not needed except

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not taking back his rule. The court still won't collect this payment in בבל; the appraisal only sets how much a victim may keep if he seizes it himself.

phrases.english: He said to them: It is needed only
for if he seized.
phrases.notes: He means the injured side grabbed property from the owner on his own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 50.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the purpose of the appraisal to a case of seizing.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since בבל courts don't collect, appraising is pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The appraisal sets how much the victim may keep if he seizes property.

steps.title: רבא's rule on which damages בבל collects
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows רבא is consistent: damage to an ox is collected in בבל, but damage to a person is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא follows his own reasoning, since רבא said: damage to an ox by an ox, and damage to an ox by a person, are collected in בבל. Damage to a person by a person, and damage to a person by an ox, are not collected in בבל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבא's full rule to show that his ruling in the ox story matches his usual view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What matters is who was hurt, not who did the hurting. When an ox is damaged, בבל courts collect. When a person is injured, even by an ox like in the story, they do not.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, בבל courts collect for damage to an ox but not for injury to a person, whether a person or an ox caused it.

phrases.english: Rava follows his own reasoning, as Rava said:
Damage to an ox by an ox,
phrases.notes: Read the first word as the one damaged and the second as the one who did it.

phrases.english: and damage to an ox by a person,
we collect it in Babylonia.
Damage to a person by a person,
and damage to a person by an ox,
we do not collect it in Babylonia.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that רבא's answer in step 51 matches his general rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בבל courts collect for damage to an ox, whether caused by an ox or a person, but not for injury to a person, whether caused by a person or an ox.

steps.title: Why Treat Damage to a Person Differently from Damage to an Ox?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why injuries to a person are not collected in בבל. If the reason is that ordained judges ("אלהים") are needed, the same should apply to damage to an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about damage to a person caused by a person, or caused by an ox, that it is not collected in בבל? If you say it is because we need "אלהים" (ordained judges) and there are none here, then damage to an ox caused by an ox, or caused by a person, should also need them...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the split we just saw in רבא's rulings. It asks why injuries to people are not collected in בבל when damage to oxen is. This line sets up the challenge, which the גמרא finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 52 showed that רבא collects damage to an ox in בבל but does not collect damage to a person there. The obvious reason for not collecting is that these cases need ordained judges ("אלהים"), and בבל has none. But that reason seems to apply to damage to oxen just as much, so the split looks unexplained.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? It asks for the reason two cases are treated differently.
Here it means ordained judges, the kind needed to rule on fines and certain payments.
There is not / there are none.

steps.confusionAlert: Here "אלהים" does not mean God. It means judges, specifically ordained judges, and that is why בבל lacks them.

phrases.english: What is different about damage to a person caused by a person
and damage to a person caused by an ox, that it is not collected?
phrases.notes: The words "collected in בבל" are left unsaid here; that's the point of רבא's rule from the step before.

phrases.english: Is it because we need "אלהים" (ordained judges), and there are none?
phrases.notes: The word "אלהים" comes from the פסוק about judges, שמות 22:8.

phrases.english: Then damage to an ox caused by an ox
and damage to an ox caused by a person should also need them
phrases.notes: The sentence breaks off here. The גמרא finishes it on the next amud by saying these cases need "אלהים" too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction stated in step 52 between collecting damage to an ox and damage to a person in בבל.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's distinction: damage to an ox is collected in בבל, but damage to a person is not.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the reason for not collecting injuries to a person is that ordained judges ("אלהים") are needed, that same requirement should block collecting damage to an ox too. So the distinction seems to have no basis.
